title: Permanent Deformation Characteristics of Beach Sand as a Subgrade Filler Integrating Dynamic Triaxial Testing and Machine Learning
content:
Dynamic triaxial tests, field FBG monitoring, and machine-learning analysis reveal that beach-sand subgrade deformation is governed primarily by deviatoric stress and moisture. Fine sand deforms more than medium sand, while overload and wet-side moisture deviation sharply amplify permanent deformation.


ABSTRACT

Beach sand is widely adopted as an in-situ subgrade fill material for coastal transportation infrastructure, yet the permanent deformation behavior of granular beach sand under heavy cyclic traffic loading and tidal moisture fluctuations remains incompletely characterized. This study examines laboratory and field tests to quantify the permanent deformation characteristics of fine and medium beach sands. A systematic matrix of dynamic triaxial tests was performed under varying deviatoric stresses and moisture contents, with up to 10,000 loading cycles applied to capture the complete deformation evolution from initial rapid densification to quasi-stable accumulation. The Selig model exhibited superior fitting performance with R 2 values above 0.99 for both sand types, outperforming the classical Monismith model. Permanent strain follows a power-law relationship with deviatoric stress, with an effective exponent of approximately 2.0, indicating pronounced stress sensitivity relative to conventional cohesive subgrade soils. A non-monotonic U-shaped correlation was identified between moisture content and permanent deformation: a 2-percentage-point moisture deviation above or below the optimum moisture content (OMC) increased the final permanent strain by approximately 10%–13%, driven by the competing mechanisms of capillary cohesion loss on the dry side and interparticle lubrication on the wet side. Permutation importance analysis reveals that deviatoric stress is the dominant controlling factor, contributing 38% of the predictive power, followed by moisture content (29%) and loading cycles (18%). Partial dependence plots demonstrate a convex stress response with an inflection point at approximately 45 kPa, corresponding to the transition from stable shakedown to incremental collapse. Full-scale field tests validated the laboratory-derived constitutive trends, confirming exponential strain accumulation and significant stress attenuation with depth. Structural Predictions show that increasing axle load from 100 kN to 180 kN amplifies surface deformation by 2.2 times, while a 2-percentage-point moisture increase above OMC yields a 2.8-fold amplification. These findings highlight the critical importance of strict moisture control and axle load management in beach sand subgrade design, and provide a robust data-driven framework for permanent deformation prediction of coastal highway subgrades.
